What is ordinarily called “intelligence” is for the most part no more than “intelligence material”; only “intelligence material” that has been processed may properly be called “intelligence.”
In the whole series of procedures that make up “intelligence processing,” the most important is “analysis and assessment.”
The value that “intelligence” possesses in itself is not fixed; only through timely and fitting “employment” can its value be raised and its effect brought out.

And the “employment of intelligence” has come by degrees to be valued; apart from the many techniques still in the course of development, the indispensable condition is one’s own strength. To put it in brief: if one has not even the power to make use of intelligence, then, though the intelligence be in hand, one can only cry out in vain at one’s own impotence.
During the period around the siege of Beiping this rare phenomenon did in fact occur.

From the end of the thirty-seventh year to the beginning of the thirty-eighth, the First Pacification Brigade was transferred south, and the writer, under orders to remain and set in hand the “stay-behind work,” did not travel with the unit.

What was the “stay-behind work”? During our training there had been no such course, and after our posting no such task had been laid upon us, so that we lacked any complete conception of it. Put in terms of the actual case, it should be: “To match one’s personal identity, to secure the conditions for a footing, and to prepare to carry on the work after the fall.” Our mission being the suppression of rebellion, what we had to do was, of course, the long-term struggle against the Communists.

The “stay-behind work” could by no means be carried out under compulsion; unless it sprang from a man’s own will, the result of forcing it would be of no benefit whatever. That the “stay-behind work” was hard and bitter may readily be imagined, and the weak of will, of course, dared not answer the call.
Though both the men and the matter were thus hard to come by, yet of those willing to stay behind there were still no small number.

The fellow students and comrades who had resolved to stay behind all wished to talk with me a good many times, for they had questions, and misgivings more than questions; and to answer their questions and clear away their misgivings was a duty that fell to me. Though I had not the least intent to gloss over or deceive, yet, being over-sanguine, I could not help oversimplifying the treacherous and ever-shifting great tide of the world’s affairs. Forty years have passed; and if what I said then be set against the way the facts afterward developed, little tallies and much diverges—which is disappointing enough. Yet disappointment is not despair, nor does it mean that there is never any hope: what cannot be accomplished in our generation, there is still the generation to come.

A man’s fortunes, above all in an age of disorder, are often past his own foretelling. On our unit there was an intelligence section whose three men set out at the same moment, advancing toward one and the same goal; and yet they walked three different roads.

The one among them who took the crooked road was not only held in contempt by all, but in the end vanished without so much as a conclusion—an illustration of that tale by which whoever is touched by the Communist Party turns of a sudden from a good man into a bad.

Fu Zuoyi of the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters,” being of a divided mind and not abiding by the decisions of the Supreme Command, and moved by his private designs, fought at the end of the thirty-seventh year one losing battle after another, losing troops and officers and grievously sapping his own vigor, and in truth let slip the fit moment of war; so that in the twinkling of an eye the Communist army was already at the walls of Beiping.

To say nothing of the rest for the moment: at that time—that is, on the twenty-ninth of December of the thirty-seventh year of the Republic—the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters” had in all nine deputy commanders-in-chief, commanding one hundred and eighty thousand troops garrisoned in the city and suburbs of Beiping.

In the preceding chapters I have set down separately an outline of the work of certain directly subordinate units of this unit, and of the three command rooms—the First, the Second, and the Fifth. There was besides the “Third Command Room” at Xugezhuang on the Bei-Ning line, and the “Fourth Command Room” at Shunyi county on the Ping-Gu line; and though these too had many doings worth recording, they were much of a muchness, and I do not mean to dwell on them at further length. At Tianjin there was a “Tianjin Intelligence Group” that devoted itself wholly to the gathering of intelligence; the basic personnel first sent out were but three men—Wang Zhibin, Qi Zhenping, and Guo Zizhong—and afterward they took on, one after another, several outer-ring intelligence men on the spot in Tianjin, among whom were White Russians and Jews of differing nationalities and the like.

As for the intelligence material they obtained, it was, in point of weight, of no small account. Being their sole charge, this was but their due, and there is nothing much in it to record. What is of interest is that these three men were all natives of the Northeast; all had had a Japanese education; all had served as Japanese-language interpreters in the days of the Wang puppet regime, and had worked together for a long while; and after the victory in the War of Resistance, in the thirty-sixth year, they all gave their allegiance to this unit at the same time, and this unit assigned them to work together in a single unit. It had been expected at first that they would be able to work in full concert, and that, with this unit’s fitting guidance and strong support besides, they would in time achieve some greater development and enterprise. Yet in the space of no more than three years, these three men each went his own way: one of them (Wang Zhibin), by a crossing of mischances, went over to the Communists; one (Guo Zizhong) fled to Japan, and, unable to remain there when his papers had run out, was deported to the mainland; and one (Qi Zhenping), whom the writer had recommended to the “Central Second Section” presided over by Mr. Zheng Jiemin, worked there thirty years, and died of illness in the seventy-fifth year.

Now in about the eighth or ninth month of the thirty-seventh year, Wang Zhibin, the leader of this “Tianjin Intelligence Group,” being on ill terms with his two group members—Qi Zhenping and Guo Zizhong—on a sudden impulse, saying he would quit and quitting there and then, flung down his sleeve and booked passage for Shanghai; when, all unlooked-for, the ship met a great storm on the way, was forced off its course, and dropped anchor at some place along the coast of Shandong.

This was truly a mischance: no one could have foretold that those who came aboard to make inspection would be the Chinese Communists’ public-security troops. Quick-witted though Wang Zhibin was, he could not in that moment make away with all the identity papers he had on him, and so was seized and carried ashore; and from that time all word of him was cut off, and none knew what had at last become of Wang Zhibin.

In the fifth month of the thirty-eighth year Shanghai was abandoned; the first director of the Chinese Communists’ “Shanghai Municipal Public Security Bureau” was Xu Jianguo, and in not many months he was succeeded by a second, Yang Fan. It was at just this time that Wang Zhibin, missing for close upon a year, appeared of a sudden in the city of Shanghai in the guise of a lackey of the Communists.

The Wang Zhibin of this time had turned bad—turned worse than the Communists themselves. Everywhere he went he flaunted himself, everywhere pried into things, everywhere sought out old acquaintances to borrow money of; and at the least crossing of his will he would at once turn his face and know a man no more. All the old acquaintances left in Shanghai, seeing his overbearing and swaggering air, took him for one of the “new great ones,” dared not give him offense, nor yet dared claim old friendship with him, but could only swallow their anger and keep him company with smiling faces; and whatever he demanded, they met to the utmost of their power, giving and yielding all he asked. And even so, there were still not a few who had the cap of “Nationalist secret agent” clapped upon them by him and were haled off to suffer and to sit in prison, and who, if they did not die, must at least be flayed of a layer of skin. Among these, to be sure, were many friends of mine. His every vile deed was in no way to be told apart from the doings of those frenzied, conscienceless traitors and running-dogs of the days of the Japanese invasion of China.

Afterward, by his own disclosure to others, he had come to Shanghai this time in the train of Yang Fan—and in the saying of it he affected an air of mystery, and could not contain his self-satisfaction. Only then did people know that he had indeed gone over to the Communists, and had turned the Communist Party’s “ear-and-report spirit”—their informer.

But Wang Zhibin’s fair fortune did not last—it was a case, too, of evil requited with evil: before long Yang Fan was purged in the “Three-Anti and Five-Anti” campaigns, and Wang Zhibin, following him, was of the sort of whom it is said, “when the tree falls the monkeys scatter”; and from that time he passed from sight and sound, his whereabouts unknown.

To look further into Wang Zhibin: he was also named Wang Zibin, his ancestral home Miyun in Hebei; his forebears had “crossed into Guandong” and moved their dwelling to the Northeast some generations back, so that he may be called a thorough-going man of the Northeast; and he and Qi Zhenping had, in their boyhood, been schoolfellows studying together at Shenyang. Guo Zizhong, though he had grown up in Harbin, could yet speak the homely dialect of Huang county in Shandong to the life, and was besides a man of a more honest, simple sort. Wang and Qi, on the one hand, and Guo Zizhong, on the other, had not known one another at first; yet from childhood they had all had the enslaving education of the Japanese, and for that reason their notion of country and their national consciousness were alike equally dim. It was the time of the puppet “Manchukuo” under Japanese rule; Wang and Qi, going eastward together, entered Waseda University in Japan to study, while Guo Zizhong stayed on in Harbin helping his father in trade. In the twenty-ninth year of the Republic, Wang Jingwei’s puppet Nanjing government made its painted entrance; and by the thirtieth year, when the puppet Special Operations Headquarters at No. 76 Jessfield Road in Shanghai was fairly recruiting men, Wang and Qi both returned to China and entered that headquarters as Japanese-language interpreters; and, as if by the same accord, Guo Zizhong too came in through the passes from the Northeast to “give his allegiance”; and so these three men worked together and became companions.

As the saying has it, men’s hearts differ even as their faces differ each from each. Wang Zhibin’s disposition was perverse and froward, changeable and inconstant; he was given to seizing the chance and playing the opportunist, and greedy of grand achievement; and because, moreover, his Japanese was somewhat more fluent than that of the two men Qi and Guo, in all the dealings between No. 76 and the Japanese side it was for the most part Wang Zhibin who came forward, so that among these three men he set himself up as the “foreman.” In the gaol at No. 76 he had made the acquaintance of several Juntong comrades who were in trouble there, and by reason of this, after the victory in the War of Resistance, he was able to seize the chance to help our side arrest several Japanese war criminals, such as Nakajima Shin'ichi, the head of the “Ume Kikan,” and the like; and afterward he served for a time as an inspector in the West District Inspection Brigade of the Inspection Office of our Songhu Garrison Headquarters. He knew the writer, and knew Brother Bi Gaokui and Brother Liu Yuanshen too; and seeing that he made a good showing, and that he had kept up a connection with Brothers Bi and Liu all along, this is the whole story of how, in the thirty-sixth year of the Republic, he and Qi Zhenping and Guo Zizhong came one after another to Beiping to give their allegiance to this unit, and were assigned to make up together the “Tianjin Intelligence Group.”

The “Tianjin Intelligence Group’s” work went forward smoothly in its early days, and seemed to hold great promise; but who could have foreseen that Wang Zhibin was froward by very nature—kicking and biting, most unfit for fellowship, ever ordering others about with a lift of the chin and a glance of the eye, bent on having his own way—and got on ill with Qi and Guo, and even turned to open enmity, until at last it came to a bad and bitter end, and Wang Zhibin, alone and of himself, broke from the traces and was gone.

The Wanli, run aground by the wind on the Shandong peninsula—it was there that Wang Zhibin was taken by the Communists’ public-security troops; and he underwent, it is said, a “brain-washing,” a remolding of thought, and did indeed seem to have become another man. In truth it was not that the “brain-washing” had wrought the change; it was all brought about by Wang Zhibin’s own want of any central conviction, by that bad root in him of the habitual opportunist. Knowing, as he did, Japanese in speech and writing, and being besides well versed in the state of things at Shanghai, he was just the man for these Communist country-bumpkins to use, on entering Shanghai, as an “eye-line”—an informer—in the “clearing-out of Nationalist secret agents”: a case, in truth, of “gaining on both counts.”

From the case of Wang Zhibin one may see that the difference in the education a man has received and in the living environment in which he has grown up is enough to sway him toward good or toward evil, toward success or ruin, weal or woe—it may well serve as a solemn warning.

That the Chinese Communists, with set purpose and scheming heart, plotted to seize the reins of power was no matter of a day; so that when, at the beginning of the thirty-eighth year of the Republic, they fell upon and plundered Beiping and Tianjin, it was, of course, no surprise.

From the fall of the lone city of Shenyang on the thirty-first of October in the thirty-seventh year, and the loss of the whole territory of the Northeast, Lin Biao’s forces at once, on the one hand, hastened to repair the Bei-Ning railway, and, on the other, using every means of conveyance, poured their whole army southward in invasion and in through the passes; the conscript laborers pressed into service alone came to upward of one hundred and fifty thousand men. Our army’s repeated defeats had, of course, many causes: a part of them was known to all; a part was such as only a few could know; and a smaller part still could only be set down as past all understanding, or, one might say, as lying somewhere between the true and the false. Were these to be gone into earnestly, one by one, it would make a weighty “history of rancor.” The writer’s office and station are in truth not equal to the discussing of this; I do but set down, so far as the intelligence material reaches, a little of the men and matters that bear upon it.

For the Communist army’s assault on Beiping and Tianjin, in order to unify command and leadership, in the “Party” there was formed a “Beiping-Tianjin Front-Line Committee,” headed by the three men Lin Biao, Luo Ronghuan, and Nie Rongzhen, styled in brief the “Beiping-Tianjin Front Committee”; while in the “Army” there was set up a “Beiping-Tianjin Front-Line Command,” with Lin Biao and Nie Rongzhen severally as commander and deputy commander, and Luo Ronghuan as political commissar.

In the foregoing I have told in outline the career of Lin Biao; here let me speak further of Nie Rongzhen. At this moment the substantive post of the bandit-chief Nie was “Commander of the North China People’s Liberation Army.”

The bandit-chief Nie was one of those among the Communist army who had taken part in the long-range flight; that “flight” of theirs across a good many provinces the Chinese Communists vaunt as the “Long March of 25,000 li.”

From the twenty-third to the twenty-fifth year of the Republic, from Jiangxi by way of Hunan, Guizhou, Sichuan, Xikang, and Gansu they came at last to Shaanxi; through how many encirclements and pursuits none can say—and yet the grass was not pulled up by the roots, and a mischief was left for the days to come.

In the twenty-sixth year, at the Double-Seventh outbreak of the War of Resistance, the Communist army accepted reorganization by the government, and Nie Rongzhen was made deputy division commander and concurrently political commissar of the “Eighth Route Army’s 115th Division,” the commander of that division being none other than Lin Biao. They were stationed in the region of Shanxi.

In the winter of the same year, after Taiyuan in Shanxi had fallen, the main force of the 115th Division shifted to the region of the Fen River in southern Shanxi. Nie Rongzhen, acting upon a decision of the “Eighth Route Army Headquarters”—which was in truth a scheming trick of the Chinese Communists—in his capacity as deputy division commander led one independent regiment, one cavalry battalion, and two under-strength companies, in all upward of two thousand men, to stay behind and hold Wutai; and, doing there as he pleased, set up the so-called “Jin-Cha-Ji Military Region,” making himself its commander and political commissar. Its compass was no more than the mountain districts of the two counties of Wutai and Meng. It was in this patch of ground that the bandit-chief Nie coerced the local folk, actively built up his armed strength, and founded besides a “Military and Political School” to train lower-grade military and political cadres; and, shutting his gates, made bold to raise rebellion—while all their equipment and supply were being issued to them, according to the regulations, by the government.

In the third month of the twenty-seventh year, Mao Zedong, in an address to the third session of the “Anti-Japanese University” at Yan’an, praised Nie Rongzhen’s setting up of a “base area” in the Wutai Mountains without stint, saying some such thing as, “Of old there was Lu Zhishen, and today there is Nie Rongzhen.” This was truly a case of a horse’s mouth that does not match the ox’s head.

From the twenty-eighth year onward, Nie directed his subordinate military sub-districts—Yang Chengwu, Guo Tianmin, Huang Yongsheng, Xiong Botao, Deng Hua, and the rest—to spread severally into the remote outlying counties of the two provinces of Hebei and Chahar bordering on Shanxi, and so enlarge his domain.

In the winter of the same year, Lin Biao, commander of the 115th Division, in a surprise attack upon the garrison troops of Shanxi that did not succeed, was wounded; and during the time he went to Yan’an for treatment, Nie acted for a while as commander of that division. In this period he ceaselessly launched surprise attacks upon the national army and snatched what advantage he could.

In the eighth month of the twenty-ninth year, under the planning of Zhu De and Peng Dehuai, Nie Rongzhen gathered together a force of some forty-odd regiments of his command to take part in the so-called “Hundred Regiments Offensive,” with “seeking soldiers and seeking food” for its object, harrying the stretch of the Zheng-Tai railway from Pingding to Shijiazhuang, and with a further twenty-odd regiments harrying severally the East Hebei section of the Bei-Ning line, the north section of the Jin-Pu line, the Cang-Shi line, the Ping-Gu line, the north section of the Ping-Han line, and many places besides. Like roving bandits out on a raid, they plundered and pressed men into service together, and those who came to grief were the very poor peasants trodden into the mire of the flames of war. The “class interest” and the “liberating of the people” and the rest that they kept always on the tip of their tongues, by this time had all turned to so much wind.

On the so-called “Hundred Regiments Offensive” the two men Mao Zedong and Zhu De were at variance: Mao Zedong held that this action wholly ran counter to his “strategic policy.” For he was in dread lest, through “resisting Japan,” he suffer loss and damage that hard-won mite of “vigor” he had nursed into being; and, on the other hand, he was unwilling to see Zhu De and the others take too much upon themselves and slip from his leadership. The aptest reading of it is simple jealousy. And so even the feigned fighting of the Japanese was from that time given over and done no more.

Thereafter, seizing the moment when the Japanese army, throwing its whole strength into the war of the Pacific, had no power to attend to both at once, they actively set about extending and enlarging, consolidated the several “base areas” they had already usurped, and reached out besides into the territory of the Northeast.
In the thirty-fourth year the Chinese Communists convened the “Seventh National Congress,” and Nie Rongzhen was elected a member of the Seventh Central Committee.

In the eighth month of the same year, when the Japanese army surrendered and the Communists reckoned their chance had come, Nie led his forces to harry the east section of the Ping-Sui line, the north section of the Ping-Han line, and the north section of the Jin-Pu line, to seep into Chahar, to fall upon Zhangjiakou, and to come and go about the near suburbs of Beiping, Tianjin, and Baoding, of set purpose obstructing the northward advance of the government’s takeover troops.
Their conduct was hateful in the extreme.

And there was worse than this. In the first month of the thirty-fifth year, under American mediation, the government proclaimed a cease-fire order (binding on both the Nationalist and Communist sides); yet Nie Rongzhen secretly instructed his subordinate troops to use the occasion of the cease-fire to launch surprise attacks upon the national army—not only breaking the cease-fire order, but snatching advantage out of it.

In a telegram of his to the Communist forces near Jining in Suiyuan there runs: “The Executive Group of the Executive Headquarters for Military Mediation will fly to Jining to inspect before twelve o’clock on the seventeenth. It is hoped that you will speedily order the Third Brigade and the Sixth Regiment, in concert with the friendly forces” (meaning the Communist army) “to gain time, at no matter what cost, and resolutely and with all speed to annihilate the enemy at Jining” (meaning the national-army troops garrisoned near Jining), “striving to bring the fighting to an end before ten o’clock on the seventeenth.” The local Communist forces, upon this telegraphic order of Nie’s, moved every Communist soldier at Jining and, sparing not the human-wave tactic, through the night, wave upon wave, kept up an unremitting fierce assault, and in the end seized Jining. This, then, is the Communist Party’s “representative masterpiece”; whereby one may see that in whatever is to their advantage they cast all else aside, and there is no shameless thing they will not do.

By the time the “Executive Group of the Military Mediation Headquarters” reached Jining, they falsely gave out that they had held Jining long before the cease-fire took effect. And since at that time the “cease-fire” had already been proclaimed, what was to be done, short of driving them out by force of arms? This is but one instance among many; of the like of it there are more than can be told.

By the thirty-fifth year the Chinese Communists no longer disguised their rebellious acts, but brazenly changed the designation of their forces to the “People’s Liberation Army”—that is, cast aside and used no more the designation of the “Eighteenth Group Army” that the government had conferred, and set up a house of their own. Nie Rongzhen too was no longer deputy commander of the “115th Division,” but became commander of the “Jin-Cha-Ji People’s Liberation Army.”

In the thirty-sixth year Nie Rongzhen’s forces still squatted upon the greater part of the territory of Jin, Cha, and Ji. When this brigade first opened up its work at the end of the thirty-sixth year, it was ascertained from the intelligence material that Nie’s forces had already as many as eight “columns.” One column was roughly equal in strength to an army of three divisions.

In the eleventh month of the thirty-seventh year, a meeting of the Chinese Communist Central Political Bureau resolved to divide the forces of the several regions into three grades—“field forces,” “military-region forces,” and “people’s armed forces”—corresponding roughly to the national army’s regular combat troops, local peace-preservation troops, and people’s self-defense corps. At that time the former “Jin-Cha-Ji People’s Liberation Army” was renamed the “North China People’s Liberation Army,” still with Nie Rongzhen as commander.

By the thirty-eighth year, when Beiping and Tianjin fell into the devils’ hands, Nie Rongzhen took up the posts of “Commander of the Chinese Communist North China Military Region” and “Commander of the Chinese Communist Beijing-Tianjin Garrison District.”
In the ninth month of the same year, succeeding Ye Jianying, he held concurrently the posts of “Director of the Chinese Communist Beijing Military Control Commission” and puppet “Mayor of Beijing.”

In the tenth month of the same year, when the Chinese Communist puppet regime was usurpingly set up at Beiping, Nie was made a member of the puppet “Central People’s Government Council” and of the puppet “Central People’s Revolutionary Military Commission,” and concurrently deputy chief of the general staff of the Communist army’s “General Staff Headquarters,” acting in the office of chief of the general staff (the chief of the general staff, Xu Xiangqian, not having taken up his post by reason of illness). Yet from the thirty-ninth year onward he slowly faded from view.

Such, then, was the number-one adversary of our work—Nie Rongzhen. In the ten years and more before and after the War of Resistance, in the four provinces of Jin, Ji, Cha, and Sui, the vexation he gave the national army was the greatest of all.

Setting it down thus far, I recall of a sudden: in the thirty-seventh year, in the commander’s office of the brigade headquarters in Fuxue Lane at Beiping, there hung a good many home-made charts and tables, the content of which was wholly concerned with the “North China People’s Liberation Army”—apart from designations, strengths, and stations, there were plainly marked their day-to-day movements as well. At that time, as concerned Nie Rongzhen, we had him indeed at our fingers’ ends. And yet, on this alone, it does not follow that one can win battles.

As, I believe, was mentioned in that chapter of one of the earlier volumes, the writer once, some years ago, made an attempt to write a “Treatise on Intelligence,” but afterward, feeling his own powers not equal to it, gave it over. I recall that one of its sections was headed: “The Employment of Intelligence and National Strength.” Its purport was that to rely on “knowing the enemy” alone can be no warrant of certain victory; there must be other favorable conditions to match it. And among the many conditions, the most important is the strength to employ intelligence; if one does not possess the strength to employ intelligence, then, though one come by “intelligence of the highest order,” it is all in vain—for intelligence not put to use yields no value and works no effect.

Let me take, by way of illustration, a plain and easy example somewhat removed from the actual, that no unwanted associations may arise. Suppose intelligence shows that the enemy army is massing its strength upon some strong-point; if one can strike it at the fit moment, one may deal it a fair measure of hurt and setback. But if one cannot put out a body of troops equal to the sally, then one can only watch a chance slip away.

Or again: suppose intelligence learns that the other side means, at some international conference, to take a step against us to our hurt; then our side must deal it a strong counter-stroke beforehand, for without that our own interests cannot be safeguarded. But if one cannot put out so much as a delegate equal to the charge, then one can only sigh helplessly before the vast ocean.
The “body of troops” and the “delegate” of these two examples are not to be lightly regarded: they are what is called, in the “employment of intelligence,” the “strength.”

At the end of the thirty-seventh year, when this unit was ordered south, besides myself the brigade headquarters still had some fifty men left behind to see to unfinished business; and as for the gathering, processing, and distribution of intelligence—work that could not be broken off—it had never once been interrupted.

Though our grasp of the Chinese Communists’ military and political doings could still be kept up without falling out of touch, yet on the side of the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters” little actual use was any longer made of it. Why? This shows that the strength to employ intelligence was day by day weakening.

On this point—that the employment of intelligence must be attended by a suitable measure of strength—I have spoken in a somewhat roundabout way; but one may see, at all events, the “state of powerlessness” that had by that time come to light.

A point I would ask you to mark a little is this: from the thirty-fifth year on, over two or three years, the Chinese Communists’ unit designations were of every stripe and kind, changed and changed again, until even they themselves were thrown into a muddle by them, let alone the outside world. Taking Nie Rongzhen’s forces alone, there appeared, in the news media and in the intelligence material, as many as four: “Jin-Ji-Cha Military Region,” “Jin-Ji-Cha People’s Liberation Army,” “North China People’s Liberation Army,” “North China Field Army.” As for the day this was taken into use, and the day that fell out of it, the confusion, I am sure, was very great, and there is no need to spend pains on the tracing of it. In the writer’s memory, from his many years of handling intelligence, Nie Rongzhen was at one time or another commander of the “Jin-Ji-Cha Military Region,” commander of the “Jin-Ji-Cha People’s Liberation Army,” and commander of the “North China People’s Liberation Army.” As for how true the name “North China Field Army” may be, no correct answer has ever been come by—that is to say, this “designation” may not have existed at all.

As for the “Beiping-Tianjin Front-Line Command” at the beginning of the thirty-eighth year, it was a temporary thing, and of very short life; after the fall of Beiping and Tianjin it too was withdrawn. Thereafter, when the bandit army for the most part went south, only Nie Rongzhen’s forces were left behind to watch over North China. I was just going over this passage in proof when of a sudden a telephone call came, saying that “Hong Fuyu is dead”; and because he had lived alone in Taiwan and never married in all his life, we were to talk over between us the matter of his burial.

Brother Hong Fuyu had worked, too, in the First Pacification Brigade at Beiping; the many home-made charts and tables I spoke of before, that hung in the brigade-headquarters office, were of Brother Hong Fuyu’s making. Drafting was his special skill; after his discharge from service he worked in an advertising company, and stayed there some decades, master and man well content with one another; and who would have thought that, after some years without a meeting, the sudden word I heard should be such ill news.

Brother Fuyu this year, too, was well past seventy; we had shared hardship and peril together. One year, abroad, he labored for wages to help me out—a thing indeed not easy to do; and I set down these two sentences in memory of the depth of our friendship.
The deputy brigade commander, Brother Li Yulin, stayed some days at Nanjing, and came back to Beiping about the eleventh month.

The word he brought back was this: as to the southward transfer of the brigade, our superiors had accepted our proposal; only this was a “comprehensive case,” to be settled as a whole, not the affair of the “First Brigade” alone, but with the other brigades to be taken into account at the same time. And in fact the several brigades at this moment—including the “Second Brigade” in the Northeast, the “Third Brigade” in Shandong, the “Fourth Brigade” in Henan, the “Fifth Brigade” in Shanxi, the “Sixth Brigade” that had met with grave misfortune, and the “Seventh Brigade” in urgent need of replenishment—all, besides their heavy sacrifices, stood in need of reorganizing and refitting. So that there was no small likelihood of a wholesale reshaping and a fresh reorganization.
As to what the decision would be, an official dispatch would come within a few days.

I asked Brother Yulin, “Is this then settled beyond change?” He said, “On the whole it will not alter.” Beyond that, what gave us concern was the attitude of the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters”; for between us there was a “relation of attachment,” and even when our superiors had made their final decision, we could not up and go, but ought in all propriety to go through certain forms that had to be observed. This too could only be spoken of when the time came.
The plan for the “stay-behind work” had been approved. Only, what our superiors looked for was on a far greater scale than what we had drawn up.
This was a thing that must be set about at once! The three great difficulties—men, matériel, and funds—had every one to be solved and overcome.

Writing to this point, the writer hesitates a little. Though this be an old matter of forty years ago, yet of the men left behind on the mainland, if any still survive, their average age would be but sixty or seventy; and even were there but a single one still living—who has perhaps by now sown down more seed—the writer, out of moral duty and out of a guarantee of their safety, ought to write what may be written and leave unwritten what may not; and, to be sure, there are many things that I myself, not knowing them, cannot write down either.

The “stay-behind work” was no light or easy matter; of the three basic conditions, the first and foremost lay in “men.” Such a man must have conditions enough for survival, and must besides have passed through long training; it was not to be borne merely by having courage and no fear of death. Were one to seek only a short-term, quick result, the effect may be known without the asking.
Even so, a body of men was yet selected, and of every one full consent was won, with not the least element of compulsion in it.

Think only that, in the instant each one of them nodded his head and consented to “stay behind,” the fate of a man’s whole life might be decided—what a greatness of resolve that called for! Had they had no faith at all in the struggle against the Communists and the recovery of the nation, could they have made such a choice?

As for matériel, the chief was the communications equipment, which included wireless transmitting-and-receiving sets and wireless telephones; herein were many technical questions, of which the writer understood little, but which were, past all doubt, seen to as far as could be. In this the one who lent the greatest aid was fellow student Sun Longguang; for, being by training an aeronautical-electronics man, he not only understood the matter but had many channels, so that from procurement to assembly fellow student Sun Longguang did indeed no small labor. As to the communications rules—wavelengths, call-signs, code-books, base ciphers, and the like—the planning and even the carrying-out were in the charge of the radio-station chief, Brother Li Fusheng.

The question of funds was no light one; had it not been for our good commissary officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Nie Enjun, I should have been at my wits’ end. At this time, in Beiping, the gold yuan note had no standing in the market; legal circulating currency though it was, it was no longer welcome. Still less could the gold yuan note be issued to the “stay-behind personnel” to keep against their future needs.

What was of use—that is, what was accepted, and would still hold a certain value in the days to come—were two things: the most beloved being the ugly “Yuan big-head,” and next after it, the sacks of “foreign white flour.” The “Yuan big-head” was the silver coin, the silver dollar; and though there were many different designs, it was by custom called the “Yuan big-head”—for no other reason than that the bald pate of Yuan Shikai was the more commonly seen.

Each “Yuan big-head” bore a fixed ratio to “a sack of flour”; but as to how many silver dollars a sack of flour came to, the writer cannot for the moment say. Might I ask Brother Yuanshen—do you still remember?

I do not know in detail how Nie Enjun dealt with the supply district; at one time he drew several months’ pay and supply for several hundred “operational places,” and the whole of it was converted into flour. And so, as was said in the foregoing, it filled the great hall to overflowing, piled up several feet high.

What the accounting system of that time was, I had not the least notion; and so it was I who decided to change a part of the flour into “Yuan big-heads,” to serve as the funds for the “stay-behind personnel.” As to the sum of it—from the outset there had been no “ledger”; how much in all was paid out? Not even an “approximate” could be given. Happily, from first to last no account was ever rendered to our superiors; and our superiors merely accepted the work, and never asked how much money had been spent.
If any should wish to ask—how many men in all were left behind?
With what equipment?
Who were they all—do you still remember their names?
Besides Beiping and Tianjin, were there other places as well?
What was the task laid upon them at the last?
What were the several methods of contact? And how were they to be supplied?
How do things stand with them now?

Plainly, these are all “secrets”; not to say that I have forgotten them, but even had I not forgotten them wholly, I could not tell. Some twenty years ago, I think, I once met the officer who had managed the affair, Colonel Zhang; and though I knew it in my heart, I dared not touch upon the matter—an impression that stays with me in memory; and now this officer, too, has passed away.

Yet there is one very concrete fact that, had it not been printed in the newspapers, I should of course never have known. It was about the thirty-ninth year of the Republic, if not the fortieth, that at Hong Kong I saw, in the Guangming Ribao published at Beiping, a passage of record whose purport was this: “One morning early, a party of Communist cadres of the Chinese Communist public-security department went to search a certain private dwelling; they knocked long at the door, and within, for a good while, no one answered; and just as they broke in, a shot rang out of a sudden, and then all was still. They went up to the second floor to look, and found that the dead man, a revolver gripped in his hand, had taken his own life. Presently, in a hollow in the roof, they turned up a converted transmitting-and-receiving set, and by the head of the bed, on the floor, a pinch of ashes. It was afterward confirmed that the dead man was named Ji Zhaoxiang.” Just so—by his true name and surname, unwilling to fall into the enemy’s hands, and taking his own life with a lifted gun, was the martyr Ji Zhaoxiang, who died gloriously for his cause in the “stay-behind work.” Ji Zhaoxiang had of his own accord come before me to ask to be left behind; his conditions for a footing were most fitting, and he had besides the technical skill to work a transmitting-and-receiving set—an ideal man, to be sure, not to be had for the asking. After the routine repeating-back of the contact regulations, and after the basic task had been laid upon him, fellow student Ji Zhaoxiang said, very low: “Brigade commander, might I be issued a revolver?” I asked him, “What do you want a gun for?” Fellow student Ji looked at me with those two moist eyes of his, then hastily lowered his head and made me no answer.

I did not wish to cross his desire; and though it was against the regulations, I granted it to him even so. At that time it never entered my mind that he was preparing it against the necessity of taking his own life. I close my eyes, and calling to mind the look of him when he asked me for the gun, my heart aches so that I too could weep aloud in pain.

In the several decades gone by, I have heard, scattered here and there, this and that fragment concerning the “stay-behind work”; and what I still remember now is this: that a part of it had already been broken up, and of those who were taken, all word was thenceforth lost.
Only a few, because they truly could no longer survive, were forced to flee the mainland once more.
It is said that Ji Zhaoxiang had made radio contact a number of times; but what the inner circumstances were, that I do not know.

In the period from the thirty-ninth to the fortieth year, there would now and then be a short notice or two in the mainland newspapers letting slip some word of the matter; and thereafter one saw no more of such things printed. My thought is, not that there was none, but that the “control” had grown the stricter.

The changes of these forty years have been too great; there are, of course, ever so many things past all imagining. What is beyond the reach of thought is that a man’s years of life should pass thus through a long forty years—what a strength of will that must take! Suppose there were truly one who could set before the world the course of mind of “forty years lying hid in fear and trembling”—that would indeed be a thing worth the seeing.

Of the “stay-behind work” I write no further than here. I have looked it over with care once or twice; all that is said is what may be said, and though it be but this little, in rough outline, yet it is already the most that is to be understood of the whole case. If I die, those things that cannot be told will be buried deep in the ground along with me—for I myself am the “file.”
Here I must in all earnestness set forth that what is spoken of above is only this part which I myself managed; in all reason, surely it was not “the one and only copy”? Who knows the rest?

Last, what I would say is this: there are herein many questions of imperfect “system”; but the aim of writing this book is to set down a record, and were it made too technical, folk would not be able to make it out—better, then, to spare it!

In the “Prefatory Soliloquy” at the head of the whole book “Nameless Heroes,” there is a short passage that touches on this: “Writing to this point, I call to mind an affair of thirty years ago (it should now be forty): a certain great Western power, that made a parade of human rights and professed cooperation, and would join in the struggle against the Communists, yet—with preparation beforehand not full enough, with the environment on the ground insufficiently understood, with the conditions for survival for the most part wanting, and with staff work resting upon mere supposition—would needs air-drop our working comrades, one by one, onto the mainland. Our comrades, though they showed a courage beyond compare, yet in the end reaped no gain whatever, and many lives were thrown away for nothing! This holding of men’s lives as of straw dogs, this casting-away, at no price at all, of the fair prospects of these promising young men of ours, was truly an unpardonable outrage! Among them were several comrades who had been my fellows-in-arms on that one front in North China where I fought the Communists; and the more to be grieved over is that, after their death, even their solatium money hung void, with no kinsman to claim it.” What is spoken of above is an outline of how the fellow students of the “Lizhi Class,” after coming severally to Taiwan in the thirty-eighth and thirty-ninth years, were in part selected and trained and sent once more to the mainland.

Fellow students of the “Lizhi Class” were to be found in every Pacification brigade; those selected and trained this time were not all of them fellow students of the “First Brigade,” but yet were for the most part of the “First Brigade.”

I was not in Taiwan at the time, and the carrying-out of this work was in other hands, so that I know but little of it. That I would set the matter down is, for one thing, to commemorate their deeds of valor; and again, to lament their sacrifice; and even, indeed, it carries something of a cry against injustice.

The “certain great Western power” hinted at in the text—everyone understands which country it is—that at the outset said at every breath that it was against the Communists, proved in the end but a half-baked thing; for all its advanced science, it had in truth no measure or standard at all, and in talking cooperation with it one had, indeed, the feeling of being made a fool of.

This country is too hard-headed; at every turn it talks of sanctions and reprisals, so that one feels there is nothing to it beyond profit and loss. To say nothing else: since the Second World War it has, in greater and smaller measure, more and less, “aided” some scores of countries and regions in all; and in the end, digging up what it had buried like the fox that cannot let be, it came to no good result—not a single country showed it gratitude, but rather it was left amid a chorus of complaint, a din of blame. From this one may see that there must be some fault in their way of doing things.

In the thirty-ninth year a certain “XX Company” came forward to “cooperate” with a certain intelligence organ of our government in mainland work on the theme of anti-Communism. Our side put up the “men,” their side put up the “money and the technique.” In the foregoing the writer offered four sentences of comment on this affair, which I here explain a little, as follows. First: “preparation beforehand not full enough.” This is the commonest thing, and the easiest to befall; if the situation be pressing, it may yet be excused; but where a thing can be done at leisure, all ought in reason to be attended to and made complete.

Second: “the environment on the ground insufficiently understood.” This time the objective was a remote region on the mainland; yet in fact, of the many basic circumstances that ought to have been understood about this place, there was, that is to say, not intelligence enough to support the action. Gone into, it was too rash by half.

Third: “the conditions for survival for the most part wanting.” Only if a man can survive will there be any showing in his work; otherwise, what is the good of jumping down? Could a counterfeit identity paper, cobbled up as it were behind closed doors, be made to pass? Could it deceive its way through check after rigorous check? Unless by some wild flight of fancy. How is a stranger, come to a strange soil, to strike root and put forth a shoot? Herein lies a great deal of learning.

Fourth: “staff work resting upon mere supposition.” That, jumping from the plane to the ground, one should fall square upon the crown of Mao Zedong’s head and at a stroke crush Mao Zedong to death—that too is a kind of supposition; and how much likelihood is there in it? Staff work must always have some framework reasonable and consonant with the case. I cannot make it out: to air-drop a body of men upon a desolate, thinly-peopled grassland—neither in concert with any special operation, nor gathered together to destroy some particular installation—for what was it done? There was simply no need of it at all.
Besides the four points set out above, there were many things that ran counter to human feeling and ill-suited the conditions of China; to put it baldly, they simply did not treat men as men.

To point it out once more: had this body of men, after being air-dropped, been able to bring about the looked-for effect, it might have passed; even had they suffered loss, it would at least have been “to some purpose.” But they took the means for the end, and, seeking only to be parachuted onto the mainland, counted the task therewith accomplished—which is past all reason indeed!

From what is surely known—the understanding gathered from scattered scraps of material—the brave men air-dropped were not one batch only, but several, first and last; and reckoning the number, it came near to three figures. What befell them after they went down was, however, various with each. (1) Before they had so much as reached the ground, there were already men waiting there to take them alive. No questioning was needed: one look at their gear made plain what they had come to do, and there was no getting away and no denying it.

(2) Reaching the ground unperceived, they gathered up the parachute and hid it away; but going a step further, they must, after all, make contact with the local people—and no sooner did they open their mouths than they gave themselves away; for the whole set of things prepared beforehand had been cobbled up behind closed doors, and in the event would not fit the ruts of the road.

(3) Hiding secretly among the hills and wilds, when the dry rations they carried were eaten up, they had recourse besides to woodcraft; yet even could they hold out a long while, and even set the radio going and get a message through, what use was it, when beyond reporting “seen only two or three small birds in the sky” or “a large body of horse and foot found galloping off to the west” there was nothing? At bottom they had made no contact with the “enemy body.”

(4) Now to speak of the common folk’s sympathy and their secret sheltering of them—honestly, the “situation” of the thirty-ninth year and the “hearts of men” now, in the seventy-sixth, are greatly unlike. To be sure, of those “willing in heart but wanting in power” it cannot be said that there was not one.

(5) A special instance: there were men who would rather go back and face a lawsuit than blindly make the jump! This betokened no shrinking back, but was rather a showing of courage; for they had found that they had already been “deceived.” From what the writer personally knows, at the time of the thirty-ninth to the fortieth year, if it were only a matter of “entering the mainland,” then, however tight the Communist blockade—for all that some described it as a “bamboo curtain” or an “iron curtain”—along the whole compass of China’s coastline, or by certain overland passes, one could still come and go; and reckoning it roughly, there were six or seven routes to follow, and air-drop was by no means the only way.

Here was the strange thing: we knew it, and they knew it too, and yet no reason could truly be found why it must be air-drop and nothing else. Could this too have been “psychological warfare”? Were those dropped down all heavenly soldiers and divine generals, who at a shake of the body could storm cities and sweep the field? It was too far-fetched, and passed my understanding indeed. Of things not made out at the time, some are never unriddled, and some have their day of sudden clearing; and this matter came at last to be understood—only, in the telling, it takes the heart out of one.

In the “cooperation” between the two sides, the Chinese side seemed to be in a state of letting itself be ordered about at will. Why? The causes were many; the chief was that, being poor, men’s aspirations were short; and to say that there was besides something of “fawning on the foreigner” would come near to mockery.

Of those on our side who had a hand in the affair, one must speak on two levels. The working head: his opinions, even when he had them, were not regarded, and naturally he could not but take his cue from the will of his superiors, following where they led. The chief of the unit: his standing was another thing—so long as there was sacrifice, there was a showing; and as for the actual effect, a round of “paper work” served to carry it off. What is called “red blood that dyes the button-knob crimson”—this, I suppose, is about what it comes to.

These are all things of the past now; and the fellow students of the “Lizhi Society,” when they gather together at times, will now and then talk of this matter—and beyond sighing, what more is there to say?
The time was about the ninth and tenth months of the thirty-seventh year.

Let me first give a brief indication of the general military situation. On the thirtieth of September the late President, His Excellency Chiang, came with the commanders-in-chief of the three services to inspect Beiping. On the second of October he flew to Shenyang, held a military conference to lay down the essentials of the operations, and heartened the spirit of the several commanders. On the fifth of October His Excellency Chiang flew to Tianjin, and went on to inspect the new harbor at Tanggu (which bore upon the sea-transport for the southward movement of the troops). On the eighth of October, the military dispositions in the north completed, the late President, His Excellency Chiang, left Beiping, flew to Shanghai, and returned to the capital.

Some days later His Excellency Chiang again inspected the north. For, apart from the critical state of things at Jinzhou—according to the record, His Excellency’s aim on this journey was: “first, to decide upon a plan for the recovery of Jinzhou; second, to urge the Changchun garrison to break out southward within a set time; third, strictly to press the two army groups at Shenyang and at Jinxi and Huludao to go to the relief of Jinzhou, in the hope of saving our loyal and valiant officers and men—Fan Hanjie, Lu Junquan, and the rest.” The rescue came too late, and Jinzhou fell into the hands of the Communist army even so, on the fifteenth of October.

Most unlooked-for of all was that Liao Yaoxiang’s army group of five armies, going from Shenyang to the relief of Jinzhou, had not yet come up when Jinzhou was already lost; and just as they were about to fall back to their defenses, they walked into an ambush, were set upon and surrounded, and their whole force was thereupon wiped out—a thing that struck one, in truth, as too wretched to bear.
On the twentieth of October Changchun fell, and thereupon, of the whole great Northeast, only the one isolated strong-point of Shenyang remained.

On the twenty-second of October the Ministry of National Defense issued the following account of the week’s fighting: “The national army on the east section of the Ping-Sui line, having joined forces from north and south at Qinglong Bridge, divided its troops and struck out against the bandits.

“Nie Rongzhen’s ‘North China People’s Liberation Army’—its Second, Third, and Fourth columns (field forces) and the First and Seventh Independent Brigades (military-region forces), together with the New Seventh and New Eighth Divisions (military-region forces) under Zhan Danan of the ‘Ji-Cha-Re Border Region’—had, by the afternoon of the fifteenth, been routed by our army between Kangzhuang and Nankou.”

Writer’s note: reports of this sort are much open to the suspicion of making light of the heavy: of “beating back” there was indeed some, but of “routing,” not necessarily. And in fact this too was a thing there was no help for; had they published according to the truth, would it not the more have told upon the hearts and the spirit of men?

By the eleventh month of the thirty-seventh year, the greatest battle of the whole country—the Xu-Bang Campaign—lifted its curtain. Had this battle been won, the whole course of the war would surely have been altered.

The fighting began on the eighth of November and went on until the eleventh of January of the following year, lasting all told sixty-five days. On the field of battle our valiant officers and men pressed on, the fallen followed by the living, in a sacrifice of flesh and blood that truly shook heaven and earth and made the very spirits weep! Of the dead and wounded on both sides in this slaughter there is a figure for reference: the Communist army’s casualties were four hundred and sixty thousand, and the government army’s own dead, wounded, and missing came to 304,000.

Why were the casualties so great? This was the result of the bandit army’s use of the cruel “human-wave tactic.” They pressed forward in a formation five kilometers deep—that is to say, over an area five kilometers across they packed it full of men.

Of the “human-wave tactic” there is a passage of description that says: “The government army’s artillery fire, its aerial bombing, its tank attacks, and the rest, faced with a human sea so vast, all lost their effect for very unwillingness to go on; and as for meeting them with infantry, if one broke into their positions one would be surrounded, and if one drew back they came swarming up—so that there was no advancing and no retreating, and one was thwarted at every turn.” There is this too: the Communist army, trusting to its numbers, dug a great many trenches deep and wide, so that the national army’s tank units could hardly maneuver.

The factors of victory and defeat in this battle were many; earlier writers have already discussed and set them forth, and there is no need to dwell on them. In point of strategy and tactics alone, the set of methods the Communist army used may be said to have been altogether off the road, past all talk of rule or form—what is commonly called “playing cards against the run of the suits.” This too was a point on which the national army came off the worse. And it must be said again: through the eight years of the War of Resistance, while the government with heart and soul dealt with the Japanese warlords, the Chinese Communists played their tricks behind its back, and not only snatched much advantage and learned much cunning, but drilled up in this very way certain of their outlandish moves.

To speak further of the casualties of the Xu-Bang Campaign: by the figures set out above, the two sides added together came to upward of seven hundred and sixty thousand; and supposing three in ten to be dead, that too reckons to some two hundred and thirty thousand men. In the seventh chapter of the foregoing the writer set down a passage on the “Battle of Laishui”—that one battle, once fought out, cost too its several thousand dead. Fu Zuoyi, in requital of the dead, bestowed on each a coffin; and though these were but several thousand men, yet coffins of every make and kind already filled the two or three li round about near the railway station. And the two hundred thousand and more corpses of this fierce fighting—over how much of the earth would they be spread?
What is called “bones heaped into a hill,” looked at thus, was then no figure of speech.

The above is written only now, with reference to certain materials and with a little of my own understanding added; at that time, in the thirty-seventh year, a man of the writer’s “stratum,” or take it a notch higher, would not have known of the doings on the other fronts.
Look again at the North China war-situation: on the eleventh and twelfth of October in the thirty-seventh year, there was bloody fighting in the outskirts of Taiyuan in Shanxi.

On the tenth of November, Baoding in Hebei hung isolated, its air transport cut off. A week later the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters” at last set forth the reasons for the withdrawal from Baoding.

On the Ping-Sui line: in the seventh chapter of the foregoing I told the tragic outline of how Fu Zuoyi’s main force, the 35th Army, was hemmed in at Xinbao’an, its ammunition spent and its provisions gone, the whole army destroyed, and its commander Guo Jingyun killing himself to die at his post.

At that time (the eleventh month of the thirty-seventh year), when the 35th Army was hemmed in, the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters” had ordered An Chunshan, commander of the Provisional Third Army, to lead his forces to the rescue.

The 35th Army and the Provisional Third Army were both Fu Zuoyi’s own men, and were besides his two strongest fighting units; their success or failure was of moment not only to Fu Zuoyi himself, but the more so to the whole situation of Beiping and Tianjin. Let me go on, then, and begin with the going of An Chunshan’s Provisional Third Army to the relief of Xinbao’an.

With the 35th Army surrounded in the town of Xinbao’an, the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters” urgently ordered the Provisional Third Army, garrisoned at Huailai, to leave one regiment behind on guard and with all its strength attack westward along the highway; and ordered besides the 16th Army garrisoned at Nankou (its commander Yuan Pu) likewise to send out a regiment to push forward to Kangzhuang, by way of support.

On the eighth of December the Provisional Third Army, with a force of five regiments and under cover of the air force, first drove fiercely upon Tumu Fort, met the stubborn resistance of the “Ji-Cha-Re Military Region” bandit forces before it, and was thrown back. It then went round by another way and struck at Songjiaying, southeast of Xinbao’an; and at first this went smoothly, and it came at one point to within but ten kilometers of Xinbao’an, and answered the 35th Army within the town of Xinbao’an with the fire of its guns.

Guo Jingyun, commander of the 35th Army, seeing the relief force come up, at once assigned a division to charge fiercely upon the bandit positions east of the town. But unlooked-for, the bandit forces would not leave off their close grappling; the two sides came to hand-to-hand blows, and fierce though the fighting was, no breach could be beaten open.

The Provisional Third Army, striking westward, likewise fought the bandit forces without cease; yet the 35th Army awaiting relief and the Provisional Third Army coming to relieve it were still some li apart, and fight and struggle to the death as they might, they simply could not join hands.
Thus they stood at bay for some hours, until the several armies could not but fall back to their former ground and await the moment to make another dash.

At this moment the advance army group of Lin Biao’s “Northeast Field Army,” after a forced march of some days and nights without pause or rest, on the morning of the eighth of December—its leading Fourth Column—had already crossed the Ping-Gu line and appeared in the region of Kangzhuang and Badaling on the Ping-Sui line.

Fu’s 35th Army and Provisional Third Army had a brilliant record of battle and had seldom lost; they may be called the two strongest crack brigades among all the combat forces under the command of the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters,” and were besides well able to suit themselves to the natural environment of this region. And so the bandit forces looked on them as formidable foes, and had of course long meant to destroy them; and now, when they could hem them in from a position of advantage, they were the less willing to let go.

By now the bandit forces that had appeared on the east section of the Ping-Sui line were, first and last: three to four columns of Nie Rongzhen’s “North China Field Army,” two divisions of the “Ji-Cha-Re Military Region,” and three columns of the “Northeast Field Army” that had come by forced marches to join the fight (afterward increased to six columns). The strength of these three parts, added together, was about one hundred and fifty thousand men. On the national-army side, apart from the beleaguered 35th Army of some twenty thousand and the relieving Provisional Third Army of under twenty thousand, together with the four battalions of the 16th Army not yet thrown into the fight, the whole came to no more than forty thousand—in point of numbers, about seven to two. The disparity of strength was great, and being in many ways on the defensive, they could hardly hope to win.

The “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters,” to avoid treading again the ruts of the overturned cart, urgently ordered the four battalions of the 16th Army to withdraw from Kangzhuang back to Nankou, and the Provisional Third Army to withdraw, by way of Huailai, Zhenbiancheng, and Mentougou, back to Beiping.

On the night of the eighth of December, the 16th Army, before Lin Biao’s Fourth Column had closed its ring, got back to Nankou with but slight loss. The next day it was ordered to give up the several points of Kangzhuang, Nankou, and Changping, and shift to Beiping.

The Provisional Third Army at Songjiaying, southeast of Xinbao’an, on receiving the order, withdrew through the night to Huailai. Past noon on the ninth, carried by motor-truck, it set out from Huailai along the long, narrow mountain defile by Zhenbiancheng toward Beiping. On the morning of the tenth, when the leading troops had reached Zhenbiancheng, the commander An Chunshan, out of pity for the over-weariness of his men, did not follow his superiors’ instruction to go round by Mentougou, but took it upon himself to cut by the shorter road, meaning to pass through the Miaofeng Mountains and make straight for the western suburbs of Beiping.

Lin Biao’s Fourth Column, having pushed up to the region of Badaling, on suddenly finding that the national army at Huailai had the look of withdrawing eastward, did not wait for the Eleventh Column, its partner in the action, to come up in full; its commander, Wu Kehua, leaving a small part at Badaling for liaison and watch, took a division besides (each column commonly holding three divisions) and by a bypath made straight for the pass in the Great Wall—Hengling—to lay an ambush and cut them off. Of this move the Provisional Third Army knew nothing.

On the afternoon of the tenth of December, the head of the Provisional Third Army’s motor column (in single file, truck behind truck), having come to a point about three kilometers west of the Miaofeng Mountains, was of a sudden set upon by the bandit forces on the high ground to the north; the flung stones flew wild, and the truck column, penned in the narrow way, had no room at all to turn, and the more so as the mountains rose sheer on either hand, so that the troops could hardly spread out. And thus, caught in the ambush, it took the full brunt of the blow.

In the general confusion men and vehicles dashed and collided one with another, and only after some hours did it force its way, with much ado, to the Miaofeng Mountains—where the division of the bandit Fourth Column that lay in ambush near Hengling had long since, fresh and waiting on the weary, set its array in order.

The whole army’s loss was heavy; of those who could break out singly and return to Beiping there were but a thousand and more. The Provisional Third Army’s defeat was ill worth it indeed; had it not been for Fu Zuoyi’s irresolution, with a little of his private designs added, it would not have come to collapse so fast and so grievously.

At this time the writer was still at Beiping, engaged in the handling of the “stay-behind work.” It may be that, from my whole mind being bent on it, of such things as happened above the impression is very faint, and to this day I cannot clearly recall whether it was that I “paid no heed” or that I “heard nothing at all.”

Perhaps it was that the news was blockaded, and the papers gave no report of it at all; for if intelligence had said that Lin Biao’s forces from the Northeast had already come in through the passes, and had reached the Miaofeng Mountains, it would have been a mere marvel-tale, and hard indeed to believe.

The Miaofeng Mountains, not far from the western suburbs of Beiping, held a temple fair every year about the third and fourth months by the lunar calendar. The folk of Beiping had, many of them, the custom of going up the mountain to burn incense, bringing the old and leading the young. A few of the deeply superstitious—or, one might say, the devout enough—who at every step made a kowtow, from Xizhimen at Beiping all the way to the Miaofeng Mountains, were also to be seen from time to time, and counted no great wonder.

Once the incense season at the Miaofeng Mountains came round, two things would appear in the great streets and little lanes of the city of Beiping, both brought back from the burning of incense. One was the hand-tied pinwheel, made of sorghum stalk (kaoliang stalk simply worked, also called “gedang”) and little slips of paper dyed red and green, whose whole charm was but this, that at a breath of wind it would turn. The children of poor families, though they could buy only a small one to hold in the hand, were glad enough at heart for all that.

The other was the great string of “shanlihong” (also called the “big candied-haws stick”), that is, hawthorns strung on a willow withe. How big, then, was this so-called “great string”? That is just the point. Put it thus: the large size ran above a zhang in length, and the small was five or six chi. This was unlike the finely-made “candied haws”: the candied haws commonly seen in the market are dipped in rock sugar, and besides hawthorn have crab-apple and water-chestnut and the like; whereas this kind of great string of “shanlihong” had but the one thing, hawthorn dipped in malt sugar. The freshly-cut willow withe is springy, thick at one end and thin at the other, and the hawthorns strung upon it are of differing sizes, the thick end being about the size of a finger—think of it, how big a single shanlihong was!

A battle, though it leave its traces, will not leave too many nor for too long; but the customs of the folk may hold a hundred years, a thousand years, unchanged. It is said that at the Miaofeng Mountains near Beiping, under Communist rule, the incense fires burn on as before; I wonder whether there are still the pinwheels the children play with, and the great strings of “shanlihong,” not so very good to eat, borne upon the shoulder?

A few idle words in longing for one’s native soil may pass, too, for a pouring-out of feeling. But let that be. I recall that at the end of the thirty-seventh year I received, all of a sudden, a private letter written to me by Mr. Hou Teng, deputy director of the Second Bureau of the Ministry of National Defense—yet the content of the letter was official business.

I did not know Mr. Hou Feixia, and had never had any dealings with him, and I was greatly astonished. The purport of the letter was: were I to be transferred to succeed Shi Hong as major-general chief of the Third Department of the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters,” did I agree or not?

I thought: if this were the wish of Mr. Zheng, the director, he had only to tell me plainly and outright—why go through Deputy Director Hou to seek my consent? Moreover Mr. Zheng was at that very time bidding me make a good work of the “stay-behind work,” and would not be moving me from my post at such a time!

To speak my inmost mind, I truly had no wish to go: for one thing, the ways of the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters” were hard to suit oneself to; for another, at this moment, with all in confusion everywhere, it was no fit time either. Over this matter I took counsel with Brother Liu Yuanshen, and resolved of my own accord to write to Mr. Zheng, making plain that I truly had no wish to go to the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters,” and hoping that no transfer be made.

One point, at the time, I did not think of: that after the “First Pacification Brigade” had been settled for the southward transfer, the whole “Pacification Corps” would be reorganized, with changes too in personnel, and that the moving of me to the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters” was perhaps an arrangement for my own future place and prospects.
Before long Mr. Zheng replied to me that the notion had been given up, and bade me set about the “stay-behind work” with an easy mind.

It is a great joke to tell: according to what the Tianjin Dagong Bao printed on the eleventh of December in the thirty-seventh year: “The Ministry of National Defense has formed a ‘Youth National Salvation Corps,’ appointing Hu Gui as its head, to organize, out of the ‘Suppression Corps,’ the ‘Pacification Corps,’ and the ‘People’s Service Corps,’ the exile youth to take part in the work of suppressing rebellion and saving the nation.” I read the Dagong Bao every day—how was it that I never saw this piece of news? Not only did I not know at the time that the “Pacification Corps” had been reorganized; through decades on end, save that at Ningbo I learned I had been promoted to be its “deputy corps commander,” of the rest I remained, from first to last, in a muddle, and asked no more.
